content: 1. Methadone maintenance therapy (MMT) initiated four months prior to release from prison, with a standardized dose escalation starting at 5 mg daily and increasing weekly by 5 mg until reaching 80 mg/day or until cravings were satisfied, has been shown to effectively maintain HIV outcomes and potentially reduce HIV-associated morbidity and mortality. Participants were followed for 12 months post-release at MMT clinics within 25 kilometers of the prison. Higher doses of MMT at the time of release were associated with greater retention in MMT programs after reintegration into the community. 2. In India, retention rates for opioid substitution therapy (OST) clients in prison settings were reported at 98%. Significant reductions were observed in the severity of drug dependence, cravings, and withdrawal symptoms. Additionally, decreases in high-risk behaviors, such as injecting drug use, needle sharing, and unsafe sexual activities, were noted. Prison authorities also reported improvements in inmates' health and personal hygiene. Challenges included unpredictable prisoner stays, lack of linkage to community programs upon release, and frequent staff turnover. 3. In the USA, an intensive 30-hour jail/community-based intervention significantly reduced the odds of substance dependence one year post-release compared to a single jail-based discharge planning session. Participants were also referred to optional services at community-based organizations (CBOs), and the use of these services independently contributed to reduced substance dependence. 4. Well-designed HIV/AIDS education programs in prisons have been shown to improve prisoners' knowledge about HIV/AIDS. Studies across various countries, including lowand middle-income nations, highlight the need for such programs. While knowledge alone is insufficient for protection, it is a necessary precursor. Some evaluations have indicated self-reported behavioral changes, particularly after release, as a result of prison-based educational initiatives. However, the overall effectiveness of these programs in reducing HIV transmission among prisoners remains unclear. 5. Peer-based HIV education programs have been recommended to reduce stigma and increase knowledge about HIV transmission. Comprehensive and peer-led education is critical for program success. For example, a brief transtheoretical model (TTM)-based HIV education program in Taiwan, including lectures on transmission, prevention, and treatment, as well as skill-building sessions on safe injection practices and condom use, was effective for drug-dependent inmates. 6. In the USA, interventions such as DVD-based education and enhanced multi-session programs have shown success in reducing sexual risk behaviors. Feedback suggests that interventions should be brief and simple to administer. Enhanced interventions were more effective than single-session programs in reducing sexual risk behaviors. 7. Sexual violence in prisons poses significant health risks, including psychological trauma and increased risk of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. Some prison systems have implemented measures to address sexual violence, such as documenting incidents, providing staff training, and offering post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) to victims. Structural interventions, such as installing cameras and training staff in crisis intervention, have also been piloted with varying degrees of success. 8. HIV counseling and testing programs that are easily accessible upon entry to prison and throughout incarceration have been shown to increase uptake. Voluntary testing, confidentiality, and linkage to care and prevention measures are essential components of effective programs. Mandatory testing and segregation policies are discouraged due to their counterproductive and potentially harmful effects. 9. In Jamaica, a demonstration project offering mandatory opt-out testing for new prisoners and voluntary testing for longer-term inmates achieved a relatively high acceptance rate for voluntary testing. Confidentiality and pre/post-test counseling were assured, and HIV education was provided. 10. In the USA, studies have shown that opt-out HIV testing offered within 24 hours of incarceration results in higher acceptance rates among both male and female prisoners. Prison staff preferred immediate testing due to high turnover rates. However, the lack of routine HIV screening in some facilities has led to missed opportunities for earlier diagnosis and intervention.
